AI can now help turn a published fix into a working exploit in hours. Patching still takes weeks, and for many old routers, cameras, and supermarket fridges, a fix never arrives.

"So the question isn't how to patch faster. It's how to stop needing to."

Six openings for new cybersecurity companies today, each one making patching "unnecessary, or someone else's job":

1. Live fixes: blocks an exploit on running systems within hours, then has AI write and ship the real code fix

2. An AI first responder: spots attacks without hand-written rules and contains them as they unfold

3. Per-request access: checks every request from a person or their AI agents, with credentials that expire in minutes

4. Proven recovery: keeps restoring your backups in a sealed-off test environment to prove they work, with records insurers will accept

5. An install gateway: holds and sandboxes every package, extension and AI agent tool before it can run

6. Security for the long tail: one managed service for water utilities, clinics and others that will never have a security team

Full piece from a16z's Asaf Ezra and Steph Zhang: https://t.co/y6LXgU1fbi

John Somorjai of Salesforce on what kills company acquisition deals, from attrition hiding behind ARR to a veto from the security team:

"It's really important that you're ready and you're organized so that the data is flowing and it doesn't look like you're having trouble getting access to data."

"One of the mistakes that a lot of founders are making these days is they focus on one metric alone, which is ARR. And ARR is a wonderful metric, but it masks attrition."

"When you meet with a company that has very high attrition, that usually means that there are a lot of not just unhappy customers, but there might be some product quality issues as well."

"We have 14 functions that we work with on all of our diligence processes, and security is the one function that can hold up the red flag and say, 'I'm killing this deal.'"

"You definitely want to identify the vulnerabilities before we do."

"Nothing goes better in a process when a company is totally buttoned up... But when they don't, that's when, you know, deals can die."

🚨 October Jobs Report — Key Standouts (ASKB)

This morning’s BLS release for October was a significant upside surprise across the board.

HEADLINE NUMBERS

• Nonfarm Payrolls: +165,000 vs. ~65,000–70,000 expected
• Unemployment Rate: 4.1% vs. 4.2% expected
• Avg. Hourly Earnings: +0.4% MoM vs. +0.3% expected
• Avg. Hourly Earnings: +3.1% YoY vs. +2.9% expected
• Prior-month payrolls: +29,000, revised higher
KEY STANDOUTS
📈 Massive payroll beat
The +165,000 payroll print topped every economist forecast in the Bloomberg survey, which had a median estimate of roughly +70,000.
The result was also more than double the prior month’s revised +29,000 gain.

📉 Unemployment rate declined

The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, versus expectations for it to remain at 4.2%.

That adds to the picture of a labor market that remains considerably stronger than expected.

💵 Wages came in hot

Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.1% year-over-year.

Both were above consensus expectations, another potentially important signal for the Fed as it weighs the persistence of inflation pressures.

🔄 Prior months revised higher

The report also included upward revisions to the prior two months, making the overall picture stronger than the headline October gain alone would suggest.

🏭 Job gains were relatively broad-based

The strength was not concentrated in one industry.

On a 3-month moving-average basis, payroll growth has now accelerated to +137k, up from just +28k in July.

The latest 3-month sector breakdown shows:

• Education & Health Services: +37k
• Professional & Business Services: +36k
• Trade, Transportation & Utilities: +22k
• Manufacturing: +18k
• Leisure & Hospitality: +14k
• Government: +11k
• Construction: +10k
• Other Services: +5k
• Mining & Logging: ~0k
• Financial Activities: -4k
• Information: -11k

That is a notable broadening from earlier in the year, when employment growth was much weaker and more concentrated in a smaller number of sectors.

FED IMPLICATIONS

The combination of:

• stronger-than-expected payroll growth
• a lower unemployment rate
• hotter-than-expected wage growth
• upward revisions to prior months
• and broader sector participation
gives the Fed considerably less reason to worry about the labor side of its mandate.
Instead, the report likely keeps attention firmly focused on inflation and raises the bar for any near-term easing.
That said, one Bloomberg analysis cautioned that the strength could still prove to be something of a “head fake” given broader macro headwinds, including tariffs and elevated prices.
For now, though, the October jobs report is difficult to characterize as anything other than a significant upside surprise.
